units.text: INT. EARNEST - CONTINUOUS
You really love me, Gwendolen?
units.name: JACK

units.text: Passionately!
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Darling! You don’t know how happy you’ve made me.
units.name: JACK

units.text: My own Ernest!
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: But you don’t really mean to say that you couldn’t love me if my name wasn’t Ernest?
units.name: JACK

units.text: But your name is Ernest.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Yes, I know it is. But supposing it was something else? Do you mean to say you couldn’t love me then?
units.name: JACK

units.text: Glibly.
Ah! that is clearly a metaphysical speculation, and like most metaphysical speculations has very little reference at all to the actual facts of real life, as we know them.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Personally, darling, to speak quite candidly, I don’t much care about the name of Ernest . . . I don’t think the name suits me at all.
units.name: JACK

units.text: It suits you perfectly. It is a divine name. It has a music of its own. It produces vibrations.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Well, really, Gwendolen, I must say that I think there are lots of other much nicer names. I think Jack, for instance, a charming name.
units.name: JACK

units.text: Jack? . . . No, there is very little music in the name Jack, if any at all, indeed. It does not thrill. It produces absolutely no vibrations . . . I have known several Jacks, and they all, without exception, were more than usually plain. Besides, Jack is a notorious domesticity for John! And I pity any woman who is married to a man called John. She would probably never be allowed to know the entrancing pleasure of a single moment’s solitude. The only really safe name is Ernest.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Gwendolen, I must get christened at once—I mean we must get married at once. There is no time to be lost.
units.name: JACK

units.text: Married, Mr. Worthing?
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Astounded.
Well . . . surely. You know that I love you, and you led me to believe, Miss Fairfax, that you were not absolutely indifferent to me.
units.name: JACK

units.text: I adore you. But you haven’t proposed to me yet. Nothing has been said at all about marriage. The subject has not even been touched on.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Well . . . may I propose to you now?
units.name: JACK

units.text: I think it would be an admirable opportunity. And to spare you any possible disappointment, Mr. Worthing, I think it only fair to tell you quite frankly before-hand that I am fully determined to accept you.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Gwendolen!
units.name: JACK

units.text: Yes, Mr. Worthing, what have you got to say to me?
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: You know what I have got to say to you.
units.name: JACK

units.text: Yes, but you don’t say it.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Gwendolen, will you marry me?
units.name: JACK

units.text: Goes on his knees.
Of course I will, darling. How long you have been about it! I am afraid you have had very little experience in how to propose.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: My own one, I have never loved any one in the world but you.
units.name: JACK

units.text: Yes, but men often propose for practice. I know my brother Gerald does. All my girl-friends tell me so. What wonderfully blue eyes you have, Ernest! They are quite, quite, blue. I hope you will always look at me just like that, especially when there are other people present.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Enter Lady Bracknell.
Mr. Worthing! Rise, sir, from this semi-recumbent posture. It is most indecorous.
units.name: LADY BRACKNELL

units.text: Mamma!
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: He tries to rise; she restrains him.
I must beg you to retire. This is no place for you. Besides, Mr. Worthing has not quite finished yet.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Finished what, may I ask?
units.name: LADY BRACKNELL

units.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: They rise together.

Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.
units.name: LADY BRACKNELL

units.text: Reproachfully.
Mamma!
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!
units.name: LADY BRACKNELL

units.text: Gwendolen goes to the door.
She and Jack blow kisses to each other behind Lady Bracknell’s back.
Lady Bracknell looks vaguely about as if she could not understand what the noise was.
Finally turns round.
Gwendolen, the carriage!
units.name: LADY BRACKNELL

units.text: Yes, mamma.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Goes out, looking back at Jack.
